The first thing anyone put on the empty shelf was a lemon. It sat in the middle of the board, bright as a headlamp, with a little green leaf still attached. The shelf was in the laundry room of my building, above the table where we folded our clothes. Until that morning it had held three iron scorch marks and nothing else. Nobody knew who had installed it or what it was for. The lemon suggested an answer. By evening it was gone, and in its place someone had left a paperback dictionary with the word *rhubarb* underlined in blue.

I lived on the fourth floor then, in an apartment so narrow that opening the oven door meant leaving the kitchen. I was recently divorced and had developed opinions about things that didn't warrant opinions: the correct thickness of toast, the best hour to buy groceries, which of the two dryers was more nearly honest about how long a minute lasted. The shelf interested me because it was a development. On Tuesday there had been no shelf business. On Wednesday there was a dictionary. I looked up *rhubarb*. Besides the plant, it could mean a noisy argument, especially in baseball.

Within a month the shelf had acquired a clientele. A woman from six took a green glass pitcher and returned with four good teaspoons tied together with yarn. Somebody contributed a jigsaw puzzle in a biscuit tin. On the lid they had written, “Almost certainly boats.” I took it upstairs. It was boats, except for eleven pieces of an entirely different puzzle, apparently a close view of a horse. I spent a slow Sunday fitting the horse pieces together. What emerged was one patient brown eye and enough of a white fence to give the animal somewhere definite to be.

The first disagreement concerned a printer. It was enormous, gray, and heavy enough to bow the board. A note said WORKS, which somebody amended to WORKS IF YOU HAVE THE CABLE, which somebody else amended to WHAT CABLE. For a week we did our folding beneath this exchange. Finally Mr. Bell from the ground floor brought down a cable from his private collection of cables, a collection his wife had been disparaging for thirty years. The printer printed a test page of astonishing beauty: magenta squares, yellow ladders, a whole small city of cyan windows. Mrs. Bell took it upstairs to frame.

Around Christmas I found a red wool mitten on the shelf. Not a pair. A single mitten, left hand, child-sized, with a black button sewn near the wrist. I knew that mitten. My mother had knitted dozens like it, always with a button so the pair could be fastened together by a loop of elastic. For a second I entertained the magnificent impossibility that one of mine had crossed forty years and two state lines to meet me in a basement. Then I turned it over. The thumb was beautifully shaped. My mother had never gotten the hang of thumbs.

I made a sign: “Who knitted the red mitten? I'd like to learn.” The following evening there was a reply beneath mine, in small severe capitals: “THURSDAY. BRING WOOL. NOT THAT FURRY STUFF.” This was how I met Agnes, who lived directly below me and knew me chiefly as a set of footsteps followed occasionally by a dropped shoe. She was eighty-one. She had made the mitten to test a pattern and left it downstairs because throwing away a perfectly good mitten struck her as wasteful, even if the number of cold children with exactly one hand was admittedly limited.

We sat at the folding table while my shirts went around behind glass. Agnes taught by making me look rather than listen. When I asked where the needle went, she held up her own work, waited, and let me find the opening. My first mitten would have fit a reasonably ambitious turnip. My second fit my hand provided I kept my thumb pressed flat against my palm. Agnes said this represented progress for me, if not for the thumb. By March I had a pair I could wear outside. They were gray, warm, and conspicuously the work of somebody learning.

What surprised me was how little the building changed. We did not become a family. People still abandoned wet clothes in the washers. Someone continued to cook fish on Friday nights in a manner that seemed to involve the entire ventilation system. Agnes and I sometimes rode the elevator without speaking, perfectly content to watch the numbers descend. But when a parcel for me was delivered to her apartment, she knew which door was mine. When her kitchen light failed, I knew where she kept the stepladder. These were modest adjustments. They made the place easier to live in.

I moved out two summers later. On my last morning I carried a box of possible offerings down to the laundry room: two mysteries, a corkscrew shaped like a trout, the biscuit tin of boats. The shelf was full. I stood considering my options until a boy came in with his father and spotted the tin in my arms. “Is that for taking?” he asked. I said it was, with one qualification. There was a horse in the harbor. He accepted this news without concern. In fact, he said, tipping the pieces until they rattled, that was probably why the boats had come.

My new building has washing machines in every apartment. For months I did my laundry in luxurious privacy, reading on the sofa while my socks tumbled dry. Then one Saturday I bought too many peaches. I carried three into the hall in a cereal bowl and set it on the deep sill beside the stairs. There was no sign; I hadn't thought to make one. By supper two peaches were gone. By morning the bowl was empty, washed, and back on the sill. Someone had tucked beneath it a square of paper, folded once. Inside was a drawing of a peach pit, exactly to scale.
